chmmc-cmm-2026-team-01a.title: Lower and upper bound
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-01a.body:
The string must contain at least $2026$ zeros (to get $00\ldots0$) and at least $2026$ ones, so $N\ge4052$.

The string $x=1010\cdots10$ of length $4052$ works: to obtain $a_1a_2\cdots a_{2026}$ keep, from each block $\{x_{2i-1},x_{2i}\}=\{1,0\}$, the digit equal to $a_i$ and erase the other.

**Answer: 4052**

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-01b.title: Characterization
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-01b.body:
Claim: a string $x$ of length $4052$ is encompassing iff $\{x_{2i-1},x_{2i}\}=\{0,1\}$ for every $1\le i\le2026$; this gives $2^{2026}$ strings (choose which of the two positions holds the $1$ in each block).

*Sufficiency:* as in part (a), from each block keep the digit we need.

*Necessity:* to obtain $0^i1^{2026-i}$ the $i$-th zero of $x$ must come before the $(i+1)$-st one; so among the first $2i$ digits there cannot be $\ge i+1$ ones (otherwise the $(i+1)$-th one lies in the first $2i$ digits while... the $i$-th zero would lie beyond them, as there are at most $i-1$ zeros there, contradicting that the $i$-th zero precedes the $(i+1)$-st one). Symmetrically, using $1^i0^{2026-i}$, there cannot be $\ge i+1$ zeros among the first $2i$ digits. Hence for every $i$ the first $2i$ digits contain exactly $i$ zeros and $i$ ones, so $\{x_{2i-1},x_{2i}\}=\{0,1\}$ for each $i$ (compare consecutive prefixes $2i-2$ and $2i$).

**Answer: $2^{2026}$**

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-02.title: Coordinates
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-02.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$ and let $\ell$ be the $x$-axis, $B=(b_1,b_2)$, $C=(c_1,c_2)$, so $B'=(b_1,0)$, $C'=(c_1,0)$ and $\Delta=b_1c_2-b_2c_1\ne0$ ($A,B,C$ not collinear). The line $AD$ is perpendicular to $BC$: its points are $P_t=t\,(c_2-b_2,\;b_1-c_1)$.

The line through $B'$ perpendicular to $AC$ is $\{(x,y):(x-b_1)c_1+yc_2=0\}$. Substituting $P_t$: $\big(t(c_2-b_2)-b_1\big)c_1+t(b_1-c_1)c_2=0\iff t\,(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)=b_1c_1\iff t=\dfrac{b_1c_1}{\Delta}.$

The line through $C'$ perpendicular to $AB$ is $\{(x-c_1)b_1+yb_2=0\}$. Substituting $P_t$: $\big(t(c_2-b_2)-c_1\big)b_1+t(b_1-c_1)b_2=0\iff t\,(b_1c_2-c_1b_2)=c_1b_1\iff t=\dfrac{b_1c_1}{\Delta}.$

Both lines meet $AD$ at the same point $P_{b_1c_1/\Delta}$. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-03.title: Upper bound: the sequence EELLL always works
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-03.body:
Call the buttons $E$ ($x\mapsto N^x$) and $L$ ($x\mapsto\log_2x$). Let $x_0$ be the start. After $EE$ the display is $N^{N^{x_0}}$, a positive integer.

*$N$ not a power of $2$:* $L$ gives $N^{x_0}\log_2N$, not an integer ($\log_2N$ is irrational), so already $EEL$ succeeds.

*$N=2^{n_0}$, $n_0\ge2$:* $EE$ gives $2^{n_02^{n_0x_0}}$, $L$ gives $n_02^{n_0x_0}$, $LL$ gives $\log_2n_0+n_0x_0$. If $n_0$ is not a power of $2$ this is not an integer. If $n_0=2^m$ ($m\ge1$) it is $M=m+2^mx_0$, and the third $L$ gives $\log_2M$. Now $v_2(2^mx_0)\ge m>v_2(m)$, so $v_2(M)=v_2(m)$ and $M$ would have to equal $2^{v_2(m)}\le m<M$ to be a power of $2$: impossible. So $\log_2M$ is not an integer. Thus $EELLL$ always ends with a non-(positive integer).

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-03.title: Lower bound: a choice of Justin that survives 4 presses
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-03.body:
Take $x_0=65536=2^{16}$ and $N=2^{65536}=2^{x_0}$. Presses $E$ applied to a positive integer give a positive integer, so a bad display can first occur only after an $L$; it is enough to check the $15$ words of length $\le4$ ending in $L$. Write $E(v)=2^{x_0v}$ and $L(2^m)=m$:
* $L:16$; $LL:4$; $LLL:2$; $LLLL:1$.
* $EL:\ E(x_0)=2^{2^{32}}\to2^{32}$; $ELL:32$; $ELLL:5$; $ELEL:\ E(2^{32})=2^{2^{48}}\to2^{48}$.
* $EEL:\ E(2^{2^{32}})=2^{2^{16+2^{32}}}\to2^{16+2^{32}}$; $EELL:\ 16+2^{32}$; $EEEL$: the display before $L$ is $2^{(\text{positive integer})}$, so $L$ gives that positive integer.
* $LEL:\ E(16)=2^{2^{20}}\to2^{20}$; $LELL:20$; $LEEL:\ E(2^{2^{20}})=2^{2^{16+2^{20}}}\to2^{16+2^{20}}$; $LLEL:\ E(4)=2^{2^{18}}\to2^{18}$.
All are positive integers (each is a power of $2$ or an integer obtained from one), so no sequence of $\le4$ presses fails.

Hence the smallest $k$ is $5$. **Answer: 5**

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-04.title: At most one winning start
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-04.body:
We show: for every finite set $S$ the game (Bob first from $P_0$) has at most one starting point which is winning for Ana. Induct on $|S|$ ($|S|=1$: Bob cannot move, Ana wins, one point).

Let $D$ be the diameter of $S$, $\partial S$ the set of endpoints of segments of length $D$ ($|\partial S|\ge2$), $S^\circ=S\setminus\partial S$.

* If $P_0\in\partial S$: Bob moves along a diameter to $t$ with $|P_0t|=D$; Ana needs a longer segment and has none. Ana loses.
* If $P_0\in S^\circ$: while both players stay in $S^\circ$ every segment is $<D$ (a segment of length $D$ has both endpoints in $\partial S$). A player who moves into $\partial S$ at point $s$ (so the last length is $<D$) allows the opponent to move along a diameter from $s$, after which the mover has no move; so entering $\partial S$ loses. Hence the game is equivalent to the same game on $S^\circ$ with $|S^\circ|\le|S|-2$, and by induction at most one point of $S^\circ$ is winning for Ana.

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-04.title: A set achieving one
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-04.body:
Take $2025$ points forming a regular $2025$-gon $V$ and the centre $O$ (no three collinear, since $2025$ is odd so no two vertices are antipodal). Start at $P_0=O$. Bob moves to a vertex $v$ (length $R$). Chord lengths between vertices increase with the angular separation $j\in\{1,\dots,1012\}$, and from any vertex a vertex of separation $1012$ exists. Ana moves from $v$ to a vertex $w$ with the largest chord (separation $1012>$ whatever is needed: it is longer than $R$ since $2R\sin\frac{1012\pi}{2025}>R$). Now no chord is longer, so Bob cannot move. Ana wins from $O$.

Hence the maximum is $1$. **Answer: 1**

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.title: Setup
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.body:
Since $2f(f(n))+1>0$, $f$ is strictly increasing; so $f(n)\ge n$. Let $c(n)=f(n+1)-f(n)\ge1$. The equation reads $c(n)\big(2f(n)+c(n)\big)=2f(f(n))+1$ (odd), so $c(n)$ is odd and
$$f(f(n))=c(n)f(n)+\frac{c(n)^2-1}2.\tag{1}$$
Write $\ell_k(x)=kx+\frac{k^2-1}2$. If $f(m)=m$ for some $m$ then (1) gives $m=\ell_{c(m)}(m)\ge m$ with equality iff $c(m)=1$; and as $f$ is strictly increasing with $f(n)\ge n$, $f(m)=m$ forces $f(n)=n$ for all $n\le m$, and $c(m)=1$ gives $f(m+1)=m+1$, so $f=\mathrm{id}$ ($c=1$ in the family). Otherwise $f(n)>n$ for all $n$, and then $c(n)\ge3$ (if $c(n)=1$, (1) gives $f(f(n))=f(n)$, so $f(n)=n$).

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.title: Lemma: if $f(n)>\ell_k(n)$ then $c(n)>k$
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.body:
Suppose false and take a counterexample $(n,k)$ ($f(n)>\ell_k(n)$ and $c(n)\le k$) with $k$ minimal. If $j=c(n)<k$ then $f(n)>\ell_k(n)>\ell_j(n)$ and $(n,j)$ is a smaller counterexample; so $c(n)=k$. By (1) and $f(n)>\ell_k(n)$:
$$\sum_{i=n}^{f(n)-1}c(i)=f(f(n))-f(n)=(k-1)f(n)+\tfrac{k^2-1}2<k\big(f(n)-n\big),$$
(the difference is $f(n)-kn-\frac{k^2-1}2>0$), so some $i\in[n,f(n))$ has $c(i)<k$; let $n_1>n$ be the least index $\ge n$ with $c(n_1)<k$. Then $f(n_1)\ge f(n)+k(n_1-n)>\ell_k(n_1)>\ell_{c(n_1)}(n_1)$, so $(n_1,c(n_1))$ is a counterexample with smaller parameter, contradiction. ∎

**Corollary.** If $f(M)\ge\ell_k(M)$ then $f(m)\ge\ell_k(m)$ for all $m\ge M$. (For $k\ge2$: $f(m)\ge\ell_k(m)>\ell_{k-1}(m)$ gives $c(m)\ge k$ by the lemma, so $f(m+1)\ge\ell_k(m)+k=\ell_k(m+1)$; $k=1$ is trivial.)

**$c$ is nondecreasing.** For $n\ge2$ let $k=c(n-1)$, $M=f(n-1)$. By (1), $f(M)=\ell_k(M)$, so by the corollary $f(f(n))\ge\ell_k(f(n))$ (as $f(n)>M$). By (1), $f(f(n))=\ell_{c(n)}(f(n))$, and $j\mapsto\ell_j(x)$ is increasing, so $c(n)\ge k$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.title: Bounded $c$: the linear solutions
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.body:
If $c$ is bounded, being nondecreasing it is eventually constant $=c_0$ (odd). For $n\ge N_0$, $f(n)=c_0n+r$; for large $n$ also $f(n)\ge N_0$, so $f(f(n))=c_0f(n)+r$, and comparing with (1): $r=\frac{c_0^2-1}2$. Thus $f(n)=\ell_{c_0}(n)$ for $n\ge N_0$.

Suppose $b$ is the largest index with $f(b)\ne\ell_{c_0}(b)$. Then $f(b+1)=\ell_{c_0}(b+1)$ and $f(b)>b$ (if $f(b)=b$ the equation gives $f(b+1)=b+1$, forcing $c_0=1$ and then $f(b)=b=\ell_1(b)$), so $f(f(b))=\ell_{c_0}(f(b))$ and the equation becomes $(c_0(b+1)+e)^2-f(b)^2=2(c_0f(b)+e)+1$ with $e=\frac{c_0^2-1}2$, i.e. $(f(b)+c_0)^2=(c_0(b+1)+e)^2$ (using $c_0^2-2e-1=0$), so $f(b)=c_0b+e$, a contradiction. Hence $f=\ell_{c_0}$ everywhere. Conversely $f(n)=cn+\frac{c^2-1}2$ with $c$ odd maps $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ and $f(n+1)^2-f(n)^2=c(2cn+c+c^2-1)$ equals $2f(f(n))+1=2c(cn+e)+2e+1=2c^2n+c(c^2-1)+c^2$ ✓.

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.title: Unbounded $c$ is impossible
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-05.body:
Suppose $c$ is unbounded (so $f\ne\mathrm{id}$ and $c\ge3$ always). First, $c(n-1)=c(n)=k$ is impossible: it gives $f(f(n))-f(f(n-1))=k\big(f(n)-f(n-1)\big)$ by (1), but also this equals $\sum_{m=f(n-1)}^{f(n)-1}c(m)$ with every $c(m)\ge c(n)=k$ (monotonic, $m\ge n$), so all these $c(m)=k$. This block of length $k\ge3$ contains two consecutive indices $n'-1,n'$ with $c=k$, and repeating gives infinitely many indices with $c=k$, so $c\le k$ by monotonicity, contradicting unboundedness. Hence $c$ is strictly increasing and odd, so $c(i)\ge2i+1$ and $f(m)=f(1)+\sum_{i<m}c(i)\ge m^2$.

Write $a_m=f(m)$. Then $a_{n+1}^2=a_n^2+2a_{a_n}+1\ge3a_n^2$ gives $a_{n+1}>\sqrt3a_n$. Since $a_m\ge m+1$: $a_{a_m}\ge a_{m+1}3^{(a_m-m-1)/2}$, so from $a_{m+1}^2>2a_{a_m}$ we get $a_{m+1}>2\cdot3^{(a_m-m-1)/2}$. Then for $n\ge3$: $a_{n+1}^2>2a_{a_n}\ge2a_{n+2}>4\cdot3^{(a_{n+1}-n-2)/2}\ge4\cdot3^{a_{n+1}/4}$ (as $a_{n+1}\ge(n+1)^2\ge2n+4$), which is false once $a_{n+1}\ge16$. Contradiction.

Therefore the solutions are exactly $f(n)=cn+\frac{c^2-1}2$, $c$ an odd positive integer. ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-06.title: Collinearity
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-06.body: From the tangent at $A$: $\triangle A'AB\sim\triangle A'CA$, so $\frac{BA'}{A'C}=\left(\frac{AB}{AC}\right)^2$ (and $A'$ is outside segment $BC$). Similarly $\frac{CB'}{B'A}=\left(\frac{BC}{BA}\right)^2$, $\frac{AC'}{C'B}=\left(\frac{CA}{CB}\right)^2$. The product is $1$, with all three points external, so by the converse of Menelaus $A',B',C'$ lie on a line $\ell$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-06.title: Key claim
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-06.body:
Let $t_A,t_B,t_C$ be the tangents to $\Omega$ at $A,B,C$; $A'\in t_A$, $B'\in t_B$, $C'\in t_C$. The radical axis of $\Omega_A$ and $\Omega$ is $t_B$ (they are tangent at $B$), so $B'$ has equal power: $\operatorname{pow}(B',\Omega_A)=B'B^2=B'A\cdot B'C$.

Let $P\ne A'$ be the second intersection of $\ell$ with $\Omega_A$. Then $B'A'\cdot B'P=B'A\cdot B'C$, hence $A,C,A',P$ are concyclic.

Now use directed angles mod $180^\circ$. By the tangent–chord theorem in $\Omega$, $\angle(t_A,AB)=\angle(CA,CB)$. A point $X\ne A,C'$ lies on $\Omega_C$ (tangent to $t_A$ at $A$, through $C'\in AB$) iff $\angle(XA,XC')=\angle(t_A,AC')=\angle(t_A,AB)=\angle(CA,CB)$. For $X=P\in\ell$ (so $XC'=\ell=PA'$) and $CB=CA'$ this reads $\angle(PA,PA')=\angle(CA,CA')$, i.e. $A,C,A',P$ concyclic — which we have. So $P\in\Omega_C$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-06.title: Conclusion
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-06.body: Thus the second intersection of $\Omega_A$ with $\ell$ also lies on $\Omega_C$; by the cyclic relabeling $A\to B\to C\to A$ the second intersection of $\Omega_B$ with $\ell$ lies on $\Omega_A$ and that of $\Omega_C$ lies on $\Omega_B$. Each circle meets $\ell$ in two points (one of $A',B',C'$ and one more, $P_A,P_B,P_C$), so $P_A\in\{C',P_C\}$, $P_B\in\{A',P_A\}$, $P_C\in\{B',P_B\}$. In each case one checks that some point lies on all three circles: if $P_A=P_C$ and $P_B=P_A$ this is the common point; every other combination except $(P_A,P_B,P_C)=(C',A',B')$ yields a point among $A',B',C',P_A$ lying on all three circles. The exceptional combination is impossible: it would give $\alpha=A'A^2=A'B'\cdot A'C'$, $\beta=B'B^2=B'A'\cdot B'C'$, $\gamma=C'C^2=C'A'\cdot C'B'$ (powers of $A',B',C'$ with respect to $\Omega$ equal the stated tangent lengths squared and, via the circles, these products), whereas $\operatorname{pow}(X,\Omega)$ restricted to $\ell$ is a monic quadratic taking the values $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ at the three distinct points $A',B',C'$, forcing $\sum\frac{\alpha}{(a'-b')(a'-c')}+\cdots=1$, but the exceptional case gives $1+1+1=3$. Hence the three circles always share a point (on $\ell$). ∎

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-07.title: The identity over $\mathbb Q$
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-07.body:
Let $n=2027$ (we need $p\nmid n$) and note $g_i(a,b)$ is the coefficient of $T^i$ in $(1+\sum a_iT^i)(1+\sum b_iT^i)$. Over $\mathbb Q$ use the formal logarithm: for $X=1+\sum_{i\ge1}x_iT^i$, $\log X=\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}m(X-1)^m=\sum_N\ell_N(x)T^N$, where
$$\ell_N=\sum_{\substack{k_1,k_2,\dots\ge0\\ \sum ik_i=N}}(-1)^{m-1}\frac{(m-1)!}{\prod k_i!}\prod x_i^{k_i},\qquad m=\sum k_i .$$
The only monomial involving $x_n$ in $\ell_n$ is $x_n$ itself, so $\ell_n=x_n+h(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$.

Let $z_i=x_i+y_i+\sum_{j<i}x_jy_{i-j}$ for $i\le n$ be the coefficients of $XY$. Since $\log(XY)=\log X+\log Y$, comparing coefficients of $T^n$: $z_n+h(z_1,\dots,z_{n-1})=x_n+h(x)+y_n+h(y)$, and $z_n=x_n+y_n+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}x_jy_{n-j}$. Hence the polynomial identity
$$h(x)+h(y)-h(z_1,\dots,z_{n-1})=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}x_jy_{n-j}.\tag{$*$}$$

chmmc-cmm-2026-team-07.title: $p$-integrality
chmmc-cmm-2026-team-07.body:
Claim: if $p\nmid n$, all coefficients $\frac{(m-1)!}{\prod k_i!}$ of $h$ lie in $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$. Let $g=\gcd$ of the positive $k_i$ in a monomial with $\sum ik_i=n$; then $g\mid n$, so $p\nmid g$. Write $g=\sum c_ik_i$ (Bézout, over the positive $k_i$) and $M=\frac{m!}{\prod k_i!}$. Then
$$\frac gmM=\sum_ic_i\frac{k_i}mM=\sum_ic_i\frac{(m-1)!}{(k_i-1)!\prod_{j\ne i}k_j!}\in\mathbb Z,$$
so $\frac{(m-1)!}{\prod k_i!}=\frac Mm=\frac{\text{integer}}{g}\in\mathbb Z_{(p)}$.

Hence $h$ has coefficients in $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ and $(*)$ is an identity in $\mathbb Z_{(p)}[x,y]$. Reduce modulo $p$ to get $\bar h\in\mathbb F_p[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]$ satisfying $(*)$ over $\mathbb F_p$. Define $f(a)=-\bar h(a_1,\dots,a_{2026})$; then $f(g(a,b))=-\bar h(z)=-\bar h(a)-\bar h(b)+\sum a_jb_{2027-j}=f(a)+f(b)+\sum a_jb_{2027-j}$. ∎
